 Key takeaways from Monday
 • Red-state rally: President Donald Trump shrugged off any concerns about the Republican candidate not winning Mississippi’s Senate seat, even as his very presence in the ruby-red state underscored GOP concerns about once-safe seats. “I can’t take a chance,” he said at the event for Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith.
 • Judges weigh in: A federal appeals court rejected the Trump administration’s attempt to force California to set aside votes from 20,000 people it claims are noncitizens. Another federal judge hinted she will rule quickly in a lawsuit brought by the Justice Department seeking to potentially block certification of Alaska’s Senate race.
 • Minnesota controversy: Meanwhile, Democratic Rep. Ilhan Omar participated in an event with controversial left-wing Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, dividing Minnesota Democrats. Before taking the stage, Piker shrugged off criticism from some senior Democrats.
 • Votes already in: More than 30 million votes have already been cast with just over a week to go until Election Day. This is several days ahead of the pace in 2022.

 Ted Cruz and Tim Scott warn Republican voters in SC: Democrats will go after Trump
 By Manu Raju and Alison Main in Myrtle Beach
 GOP senators warned a room of South Carolina Republicans on Monday night that Democrats will go after President Donald Trump relentlessly if they control Congress for his final two years in the White House.
 “If these lunatics take over, we will see no legislation move the United States Senate. We will see two years of impeachment circus. You will see a relentless assault on President Trump, on his family, on the cabinet,” Sen. Ted Cruz said.
 Cruz and other prominent national Republicans are in Myrtle Beach rallying support behind Sen. Darline Graham, who is running as Trump’s hand-selected pick to serve a full term in her late brother’s Senate seat.
 GOP groups have pumped money into South Carolina over the past few weeks as concerns grow that the race against Democratic Annie Andrews is too close for comfort in the state that Trump won three times by double digits.
 “The radical left has put a bullseye on your state,” Cruz said, adding, “Why am I here in South Carolina tonight? Because the Senate race for Darlene Graham is neck and neck.”
 Sen. Tim Scott, the chairman of the Senate GOP campaign arm, cautioned that a “dark, insidious force from the far left” was “lurching across this country,” highlighting Democrats in battleground races that Republicans are trying to paint as too radical to serve in Congress.
 After railing against James Talarico and Abdul El-Sayed, the respective Democratic Senate candidates in Texas and Michigan, Scott claimed Andrews is “as radical, dangerous, and weird as the two other candidates I mentioned.”
 Touting Graham’s record in the Senate, Scott noted that “in less than three months, Darline was able to pass legislation signed by the president of the United States.”
 Shortly after taking office, Graham introduced a Russia sanctions bill named after her brother, Lindsey, who championed cracking down on countries that purchased Russian oil and gas.
 Though the legislation passed by bipartisan majorities in both chambers and signed into law, Trump has since rolled back some sanctions on Russian diesel as he attempts to drive down fuel prices ahead of the midterms.

 Trump rallies in Mississippi, saying "I just got to make sure." Catch up on campaign news here
 By Pamela Avila 
 President Donald Trump throws a hat to the audience as he takes the stage during a campaign rally at Crossroads Arena on October 26, 2026 in Corinth, Mississippi. 
 Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images 
 President Donald Trump was in Mississippi to support Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith this evening — continuing his blitz through red states amid lagging enthusiasm for Republicans among voters.
 He shrugged off concerns about the GOP candidate not winning the ruby-red state’s Senate seat during the rally, but said:
 “I just got to make sure, I can’t take a chance.”
 Here’s what else happened on the campaign trail over the past few hours: 
 In a social media post earlier today, Trump seemingly laid the groundwork to potentially claim fraud in Minnesota if Republicans don’t pull out a win in the state’s Senate race. Former sportscaster Michele Tafoya is running against Democratic Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan.
 A federal appeals court rejected the Trump administration’s attempt to force California to set aside votes from 20,000 people it claims are noncitizens. Minutes before the ruling , the state’s attorney general said it was an “unconstitutional” effort to “sow distrust” among voters.
 More than 30 million ballots have been cast with just over a week to go until Election Day, according to data gathered by CNN, the Associated Press and Catalist. This is several days ahead of the pace in 2022.
 As Vice President JD Vance campaigned in Kansas for GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, he retooled his argument on gas prices — this time blaming rising costs on “tinpot dictators in the Middle East.” 
 Meanwhile in Wisconsin, former Vice President Kamala Harris told voters the elections are an opportunity to turn “anger, sadness, disappointment, frustration” into action with their vote.
 “We are now in the phase of the moment in our democracy — while we can still hold on to it — where the people’s voice reigns, where the will of the people reigns,” Harris said.
 Former Vice President Kamala Harris speaks at the third annual SHE LEADS Conference at SLS Hotel on September 29 in Los Angeles. 
 Mario Tama/Getty Images 
 Rep. Ilhan Omar appeared with left-wing streamer Hasan Piker at a campaign event in Minnesota despite state Democrats distancing themselves from him. Speaking to CNN before taking the stage , Piker shrugged off criticism and said his engaged young audience mobilizes to knock on doors and phone bank for campaigns.
 In South Carolina, Sen. Darline Graham dodged a question from CNN on the toll of the Iran war on voters in the state. While many GOP candidates in competitive races have said the war needs to end, Graham has defended the need to give Trump more time to achieve his goal of cutting off Iran’s nuclear capabilities.

 Rep. Ilhan Omar campaigns with streamer Hasan Piker as other Democrats distance themselves
 By Donie O'Sullivan in Minneapolis and Aleena Fayaz 
 Minnesota Rep. Ilhan Omar appeared with controversial left-wing Twitch streamer Hasan Piker on Monday as early voting is underway in the state.
 Greeted by enthusiastic chants, Omar sought to rally attendees to get out the vote for Democratic candidates with just eight days left before Election Day.
 “Reach out to every single person,” the congresswoman said as she referenced the tumult the state has faced amid federal immigration enforcement operations this year.
 “It would be really, really sad in this moment if Minnesota did not defeat Republicans up and down the ballot.”
 The event took place amid high security at a theater in Cedar-Riverside, a Minneapolis neighborhood widely known as the heart of the city’s Somali American community.
 Before the event, prominent Minnesota Democrats, including Sen. Amy Klobuchar who is running for governor in the state, distanced themselves from Piker, who has said that American Jews’ support of Israel will make antisemitism worse and invite violence and that America is “pound for pound as far as the number of deaths” worse than Al-Qaeda.
 “The Senator believes that a number of the statements he has made are reckless and unacceptable,” a spokesperson for Klobuchar’s campaign said.
 Speaking to CNN before taking the stage, Piker shrugged off criticism from some senior Democrats, saying he believed candidates would still want to campaign with him. He pointed to his engaged young audience, which he says he mobilizes to knock on doors and phone bank for campaigns.
 “I think it’s fascinating that I’ve become this somewhat pivotal figure in the eyes of the media,” Piker said, “[when] the overwhelming majority of Americans’ response is, ‘I don’t care, who is this guy?’”

 Darline Graham dodges question on economic toll of Iran war on South Carolina constituents
 By Alison Main and Manu Raju 
 Sen. Darline Graham dodged a question on the toll of the Iran war on South Carolina voters as she left a campaign event on Monday night.
 The South Carolina Republican, who is running to serve a full term in the seat previously occupied by her late brother, did not respond and kept walking when asked by CNN’s Manu Raju if it was worth it for her constituents to pay higher prices due to the war.
 While many GOP candidates in competitive races have stated that the war needs to end imminently, Graham has gone further in defending the need to give President Donald Trump more time to achieve his goal of cutting off Iran’s nuclear capabilities.
 She has faced skepticism about her qualifications after a gaffe in the Republican primary debate earlier this year where she admitted that foreign policy was “not my thing.”
 She told Raju earlier on Monday that she was “becoming very informed” on national security.

 "I can't take a chance": Trump rallies in deep-red Mississippi amid GOP concerns
 By Kevin Liptak in Cornith, Mississippi, and Molly English 
 President Donald Trump shrugged off any concern about holding Mississippi’s Senate seat during a visit Monday, even as his very presence in the ruby-red state underscored persistent Republican concerns about once-safe seats.
 “You know, I’m here because Cindy’s doing great, but I just got to make sure. I can’t take a chance,” Trump said.
 Trump’s self-assurance belied worries that Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith may be in trouble amid lagging enthusiasm for Republicans and an energized base of Democrats looking to repudiate the president.
 The president has been looking to combat those headwinds with a frenetic blitz through red states — a schedule whose toll was in evidence this evening as the president touted his record with a strained voice. “You know, God didn’t make your vocal cords to do a rally every day,” he joked.
 He framed his record as one of unadulterated success and made little mention of cost-of-living concerns that have dragged down his popularity.
 Trump defended the monthslong war in Iran, claiming the US had “beat the sh*t” out of the Islamic Republic and that the ensuing rise in gas prices was temporary, and pointed to recent stock market rallies as evidence that his economic policies are working, despite the market remaining volatile.
 “Your 401ks are 60% higher. So when you go to vote, and when you’re thinking about voting for Cindy — but maybe if there can be anybody in this room, I doubt it — but if you have any doubt, before you go and vote, pick up your 401ks and check it out,” he said.
 Trump did not avoid topics some of his advisers would prefer he skip, such as lengthy descriptions of his renovation work around the White House. “It actually relaxes me,” he said.
 He responded to former President Barack Obama, who lambasted Trump’s fixation on renovations over the weekend.
 “He doesn’t understand,” Trump said of the former president. “The White House has to be clean, pristine, beautiful.”
 Trump’s speech at the Crossroads Arena, in rural Corinth, was well attended, though by the time he was wrapping up, large swaths of seats had emptied.

 Judge hints she’ll rule quickly in Department of Justice's election lawsuit in Alaska
 By Tierney Sneed 
 A federal judge granted a request by Democrats that she fast track a lawsuit brought by the Justice Department seeking to potentially block certification of Alaska’s Senate race, with a new scheduling order that also hinted at some skepticism about the Trump administration’s arguments for a federal court getting involved.
 The new scheduling order from Judge Sharon Gleason, who was appointed to the bench by President Barack Obama, would allow her to rule in the case as early as the end of this week.
 Her brief order noted the events that led up to DOJ’s new claims that the presence of a candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot could confuse voters intending to vote for Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, the GOP incumbent.
 “After Alaskans had already begun casting their ballots for the November 2026 election—and nearly four months after the Alaska Supreme Court directed the Division of Elections to include Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot for the upcoming United States Senate election—the United States initiated this action on October 22, 2026,” Gleason said. 
 Gleason said she would rule by Wednesday evening on requests from the Democrats, as well as from non-partisan voter groups, that they be allowed to intervene in the case to fight the DOJ’s lawsuit. If those requests are granted, DOJ will have until Thursday evening to respond to their arguments that the case should be dismissed, the judge said.

 More than 30 million ballots have been cast in early voting
 By Ethan Cohen 
 More than 30 million ballots have already been cast with just over a week to go until Election Day.
 That’s according to data from 47 states and the District of Columbia, gathered by CNN, the Associated Press, and Catalist, a company providing data, analytics and other services to Democrats, academics and nonprofit issue-advocacy organizations and is giving insights into who is voting before November.
 This is several days ahead of the pace in 2022.
 Overall, the nation is at about 54% of total pre-election turnout in 2022, and about 28% of the total votes cast in that election.

 Vance retools “tinpot dictators" gas price remark as he stumps in Kansas
 By Alejandra Jaramillo 
 Vice President JD Vance speaks during a campaign rally at HME, Inc. on October 26, 2026 in Topeka, Kansas. 
 Finn Gomez/Getty Images 
 Vice President JD Vance campaigned in Kansas on Monday with a tweaked version of his gas-price argument, this time blaming rising costs on “tinpot dictators in the Middle East,” after Democrats used his earlier phrasing to criticize President Donald Trump.
 At a rally in Montana, Vance acknowledged that high gas prices have left some voters undecided ahead of the midterm elections, arguing that prices spike “every time some tinpot dictator decides to throw a tantrum,” sparking online backlash and social media comparisons to Trump .
 In Kansas, Vance turned the issue squarely on Democrats, saying the opposing party’s priorities had made the country too reliant on “tinpot dictators in the Middle East.”
 “Their policies are the reason that these Middle Eastern dictators ever controlled our lives in the first place, and Donald Trump and Roger Marshall are stopping it every single day,” he added.
 Vance was in the state to boost Kansas GOP Sen. Roger Marshall, who is up for reelection and facing a surprisingly competitive challenge from Democrat Adam Hamilton. The vice president tried to frame Hamilton, who is a pastor, as a Democrat who would be the “stooge” of Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer.
 “I can’t possibly know what is in the man’s heart, but I do know the lawgiver and Adam Hamilton’s world. It isn’t Moses, It’s not Jesus. It’s Chuck Schumer,” Vance said.
 Vance framed the Trump movement around sovereignty, saying it “was about reminding the American people that their government belongs to them,” and that the government ought to “fight for Americans first.” He frequently mentioned the needs of farmers, and touted that “Roger helped us unlock billions of dollars for fuel relief for farmers during this harvest season.”

 In Wisconsin, Harris urges voters to turn anger into action
 By Elise Hammond 
 The midterm elections are an opportunity for Americans who are unhappy with the state of the country to turn emotion into action, former Vice President Kamala Harris said at a campaign event today in Wisconsin.
 “For the last year and a half, I know many of us have been going through a whole lot of emotion — anger, sadness, disappointment, frustration, depression, all kinds of emotions,” she said at an event in support of Democratic gubernatorial candidate David Crowley.
People have been feeling powerless and hopeless, like they can’t do anything to make a change, Harris said, but “that phase is over.”
“We are now in the phase of the moment in our democracy — while we can still hold on to it — where the people’s voice reigns, where the will of the people reigns,” Harris said.
 The former vice president, who lost a presidential bid to President Donald Trump in 2024, called the current administration the “most callous and corrupt and incompetent” in the history of America.
 She is back in the key presidential battleground state as she weighs another run for the White House in 2028. Much of the political insider world has been clear in not wanting Harris to run again for president, yet with her midterm stops across the country in recent weeks, she’s hearing from many Democratic campaigns who believe having her around helps.
 Two years after losing, Harris said if she runs again her motivation will be to “ actually do the job .”
 CNN’s Edward-Isaac Dovere contributed reporting to this post.

 Jim Jordan remains elusive about possibly running to lead House GOP if party loses majority
 By Manu Raju in Myrtle Beach, South Carolina
 Who will lead House Republicans if they lose the majority? It remains an open question.
 Will Speaker Mike Johnson actually run for minority leader, as he recently suggested? Will others mount a bid for the top GOP spot — namely Majority Leader Steve Scalise or Judiciary Chairman Jim Jordan?
 Jordan was coy when CNN asked if he would run.
 “I’m focused on winning,” Jordan said in his response to CNN today as he campaigned for South Carolina Republicans in Myrtle Beach.
 The leadership election is expected to take place a week after Election Day and will be conducted by secret ballot. Jordan, Scalise and House GOP Whip Tom Emmer all fell short in previous runs for speaker, as Emmer is expected to run for the whip position in the next Congress.

 California AG calls Trump vote-count lawsuit an effort to "sow distrust" among voters
 By Elise Hammond 
 Election workers sort ballots at Contra Costa County's election operations facility in Martinez, California, on May 27. 
 Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images

 By Kevin Liptak in Corinth, Mississippi
 As President Donald Trump arrives in Mississippi, there are few open seats remaining at Crossroads Arena in Corinth.
 On the way in, many voters said they were here because it was a singular chance to see an American president in person.

 Other rallygoers sounded less sure about Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, whom Trump is trying to help across the finish line.
 “To be honest, I really don’t know anything about her,” John Grisham, a 20-year-old student, said of Hyde-Smith. “I really should do more research on it. I was not intending to vote coming up, but I have had thoughts recently on doing my research and voting. But it’s not necessarily guaranteed to be the Republican.”
 Tammy Bond, who works in logistics, said the first two years of Trump’s term had been “bumpy,” though she said her respect for the office had brought her out to see him.
 Hyde-Smith, she acknowledged, had experienced a similar fate.
 “She’s had a few bumps and bruises a long way too,” she said, stopping short of saying whether she would vote for her: “We’ll see after tonight. I really want to listen to her.”

 President Donald Trump will campaign in Mississippi today for GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, a surprising place to have to bolster a GOP incumbent’s popularity when he carried the state by 23 points in 2024.
 But that’s just another example of the red states the president has had to campaign in, given his unpopularity has opened up new frontiers for Democratic optimism .
 With Election Day only a week away, the midterm races are heating up. Catch up on key developments from the last few hours: 
 • President Donald Trump on Monday — eight days before the midterm election — promised a $1 million payout to anyone who reports voter fraud that results in a conviction.  • Trump also spent some time defending his White House renovations after former President Barack Obama mocked the gilded makeover of the presidential residence.

 • Republicans are still sidestepping questions around Ohio GOP governor nominee Vivek Ramaswamy’s controversial campaign ad . Texas Sen.  House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan walks to a meeting at the US Capitol on July 13.

 Republican Rep. Jim Jordan did not take issue Monday with Ohio GOP gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy’s ad featuring his Democratic opponent’s estranged mother, which the state’s Republican governor has urged Ramaswamy to take down.
 “I think it’s the Democrats wanting to deflect from Amy Acton’s record,” he told CNN on Monday, adding, “Remember, she’s been called the (Anthony) Fauci of Ohio.”
 Acton served as the director of the Ohio Department of Health during the coronavirus pandemic, appearing at daily briefings with Gov. Mike DeWine and taking heat for controversial decisions such as closing businesses and requiring people to stay at home.
 “I think this is all the Democrats saying we’ve got to say anything, do anything, talk about anything other than Amy Acton’s record,” said Jordan, who represents Ohio’s 4th District.
 While DeWine and some other prominent Ohio Republicans have condemned the ad, President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have defended Ramaswamy.
 Jordan is in South Carolina this evening campaigning for Republicans in the state, including Sen. Darline Graham and Rep. Russell Fry.
